newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Flows ease in Feb, investors think staid.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Flows ease in Feb, investors think staid.

text.p: Americans pumped less cash into U.S. stock mutual funds in February compared to the month before and February 1996, with investors moving from aggressive growth and small cap funds to more conservative portfolios, industry analysts said on Thursday.
With U.S. stocks falling sharply on Thursday, large fund companies said that investors were keeping their wallets pointed at more staid growth and income and index funds.

"The money is very concentrated," said Charles Biderman, executive editor of Mutual Fund Trim Tabs. "It's not going into high tech, small cap, but going into conservative funds that invest in big caps...people invest with their eyes on the rear view mirror."
"People have had it with aggressive growth funds," said Tracey Gordon at Charles Schwab Co. "The market is acting weird these days, and people could be holding their cash in reserve."
February cash flows were estimated at $19.5 billion in February, the Investment Company Institute said Thursday.
The ICI said January estimates were revised down to $29.1 billion. In February 1996, flows were measured at $22.38 billion.
Based on early March data, the most popular Schwab sectors have been international, growth and index funds, said Gordon.

"Certain segments of the market got weaker, especially growth and momentum," said Avi Nachmany, head of research at Strategic Insight. "My assumption would be you're seeing a conservative shift in investment style to less risky."

Vanguard Group flows "remains strong and should surpass last year," said spokesman John Woerth. Vanguard investors this month have moved mostly into the giant 500 Portfolio Vanguard Index Trust, the second largest U.S. fund with $36 billion in assets, and the $17.7 billion Windsor II fund, a large-cap value fund.
In February Vanguard flows totalled $3.9 billion, down from the record $4.9 billion in January, but above $3.6 billion in February 1996.
At T. Rowe Price Associates Inc, "the pace for March is a bit slower than February, but our cash flows are still very healthy," said spokesperson Rowena Itchon.
Some of the better selling T. Rowe Price funds were in large capitalization Equity Income, Growth & Income, Blue Chip Growth and International Stock funds.
"March is shaping up to look like a clone of February," said Gavin Quill at Scudder, Stevens & Clark Inc. "We're seeing a slight uptown in domestic equity sales."

Quill said more conservative growth and income funds were the clear choices in March. "It may be an element of portfolio balancing and judicious caution," said Quill. "As the markets get to very high levels, people are opting not to get into bonds, but stay in equities, just go down the risk scale." Schwab posted net equity inflows of $608.6 million for the first 12 days of this month, with the most popular categories as international, global and index funds. For all of February, Schwab posted net equity inflows of about $1.4 billion, and $2 billion in January, Schwab said.
